Description: This research area focuses on the fundamental transformation of power systems as they transition from being dominated by synchronous machines to being dominated by power electronic interfaces. Research within this pillar encompasses the development of advanced control capabilities, services, and design methodologies specifically for IBRs, such as wind, solar, and battery energy storage. A primary focus is the shift from Grid-Following (GFL) to Grid-Forming (GFM) technologies, investigating how inverters can provide essential reliability services like voltage and frequency support, inertia-like responses, and system strength. It includes the study of IBR protection schemes, electromagnetic transient (EMT) modeling for high-fidelity representation, and the development of international standards (such as IEEE 2800) to ensure interoperability and performance. Furthermore, it addresses the role of IBRs in system restoration and black-start procedures, examining how decentralized resources can re-energize the grid following a total or partial shutdown.

Description: The stability pillar addresses the evolving physics of the grid caused by the reduction of mechanical inertia and the emergence of fast-acting power electronics. This area covers the development of new analytical tools, monitoring systems, and control methods required to ensure the reliability and security of power systems operating with very high shares of variable renewable energy (VRE). Key research topics include converter-driven stability (e.g., sub-synchronous oscillations and harmonic instabilities), small-signal and transient stability in low-inertia environments, and the development of fast frequency response (FFR) mechanisms. It also explores the necessity of moving beyond traditional Root Mean Square (RMS) simulations toward wide-scale EMT modeling to capture fast-acting dynamics. Research here aims to define new stability limits, create automated oscillation detection algorithms, and design robust control strategies that can prevent cascading failures in highly volatile, non-linear system conditions.

Description: This area examines the integration and orchestration of distribution-level resources including rooftop solar, electric vehicles (EVs), behind-the-meter storage, microgrids, and demand-side management as active assets for the bulk power system. The focus is on the 'Transmission-Distribution (T-D) Interface,' seeking to optimize how these millions of decentralized devices can be aggregated into Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) to provide flexibility and reliability services. Research includes the development of communication protocols, localized markets for DER flexibility, and advanced DER Management Systems (DERMS). It also covers technical challenges such as bi-directional power flows, local voltage regulation, and the stability of islanded grids or DC microgrids. The goal is to transform DERs from passive, 'invisible' loads into controllable, transparent resources that support the overall resilience and decarbonization of the integrated energy system.

Description: This pillar focuses on the evolution of the power system operator's environment to handle the exponential increase in data and complexity. Research explores the development of new visualization techniques, AI-assisted decision support systems, and automated analysis tools designed to enhance real-time situational awareness. It addresses the challenge of 'alarm fatigue' by using machine learning to prioritize critical information and filter noise. Key concepts include Modular Control Center Systems (MCCS), which allow for more flexible and scalable software architectures, and the integration of wide-area monitoring systems (WAMS) using phasor measurement unit (PMU) data. Additionally, this area investigates the human-machine interface (HMI), digital twins for real-time contingency analysis, and the cybersecurity of operational technology (OT) to ensure that control rooms remain resilient against both physical and cyber threats in a more decentralized grid.

Description: This research area is dedicated to quantifying, defining, and procuring the technical ancillary services necessary to maintain a reliable supply-demand balance in a carbon-free future. As traditional 'free' ancillary services provided by synchronous generators (like inertia and short-circuit current) disappear, this pillar seeks to create market mechanisms and technical requirements for new types of system services. This includes investigating ramping services for managing VRE variability, advanced frequency regulation, voltage control, and black-start capabilities. Research focuses on the techno-economic design of 'service-based' markets, ensuring that the procurement of these services is both cost-effective and technologically neutral. It also looks at how to define 'resource adequacy' in systems where the marginal cost of energy is near zero, and how to incentivize the long-term investment in the flexible assets needed to ensure grid reliability at all times.

Description: The planning pillar addresses the need for new metrics, methods, and tools to design the power systems of the future. Traditional planning processes often fail to capture the high degree of uncertainty and the complex interactions of a changing resource mix. Expanded research in this area includes integrated transmission and distribution planning, multi-sector coupling (e.g., power-to-gas, heating, and transport), and planning for extreme weather resilience under climate change scenarios. It explores the use of large-scale, high-resolution datasets and probabilistic modeling to replace deterministic 'worst-case' scenarios. Focus is also placed on the expansion of transmission infrastructure to connect remote renewable zones to load centers, the role of long-duration energy storage in seasonal balancing, and the development of new metrics for evaluating system strength and adequacy that go beyond simple capacity margins.

Description: This broad category serves as the foundational 'catch-all' for research that addresses the power system from a holistic, systemic viewpoint or focuses on classical engineering and economic principles not specifically covered by the other 6 research programs. It encompasses the general analysis, operation, and planning of electric generation, transmission, and distribution systems for industrial, commercial, and domestic consumption. This includes research on classical economic dispatch, traditional electricity market design, and the interaction of the power grid with multi-energy carriers. Within its scope are five key sub-disciplines: Power System Analysis, Computing, and Economics; Power System Dynamic Performance; Power System Operations; Power System Planning and Implementation; and Power Engineering Education.
